subject: Disease prevalence prediction for administrative area using BYM and SPDE

messages.author: 7722b91a416248df
messages.subject: Disease prevalence prediction for administrative area using BYM and SPDE
parts:
Dear all,

I am Jaehyeong Cho from Ajou University, one of OHDSI's collaborators.

We want to create large-scale evidence by sharing research results from reusable analysis codes from the OMOP-CDM database with standardized clinical database structure and medical ontology. (https://www.ohdsi.org/data-standardization/)

OHDSI has a pipeline that extracts cohorts from a clinical database (OMOP-CDM format of Electronic Health Record or claim database). A cohort is a set of persons who satisfy one or more inclusion criteria (a phenotype) for a duration of time

The following pipeline of the cohort configuration is intended to model and visualize the regional prevalence of patients included in the extracted cohort. (GIS database uses GADM)

But, the hurdle that impedes the implementation of spatial modeling is the fact that, based on HIPAA act, you can only know residences up to county units.

In this situation, the questions related to using R-INLA are as follows:

1. In Korea, national health insurance covers 98% of the population, so there is patient information for all regions. However, in case of small area, BYM2 is used because the estimate can be unstable. Is it right? code as follows:
m1 <- inla(outcome_count ~ 1 + f(ID_2, model = "iid") +
                                 f(id2, model = "bym2", graph = "BayesianMap.graph", adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE), family = "poisson",
                               data = as.data.frame(kr), E=std_expected,
                               control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE))

2. In the United States, there are only about 2,000 counties out of about 3,000 counties. We would like to model the number of target patients and outcomes from the standardized clinical data with the SPDE approach with GADM. Is it correct to use in this case? In addition, some areas may be small areas, or in areas where coverage is not covered, information may not be available. In this case, can the SPDE model predict? And, the standardized database structure of the OMOP-CDM proposed by OHDSI collaboration, but does not yet contain environmental variables or survey data, so there is no appropriate covariate x to use when modelling. In this case, should I use the following code? Also, can i consider the random effect of just 'region'?

code as follows:
===========================================================
library(dplyr)
library(raster)
library(INLA)
library(splancs)
library(fields)

GADM <- getData(name="GADM", country="United States", level=2) #Based on GADM version 2.8

#Excluding alaska and hawaii
L <- GADM@data$ID_1 == 2
counties <- GADM@data[L,]
L <- GADM@data$ID_1 == 12
counties <- rbind(counties, GADM@data[L,])
counties <- counties$ID_2
index <- 1:3148
index <- index[-counties]

US <- readRDS("~/US.rds")
d <- US[index,]

d <- d %>%
  filter(!is.na(target_count))

est.area <- c(match(d$ID_2, GADM@data$ID_2))
d$prev <- d$outcome_count/d$target_count

coo <- data.frame()
for (i in 1:nrow(GADM@data)){
  temp <- GADM@polygons[[i]]@labpt
  coo <- rbind(coo, temp)
}

colnames(coo) <- c("lat", "long")
cood <- coo[c(est.area),]
cood <- cbind(cood$lat, cood$long)
cood <- as.matrix(cood[, 1:2])


coop <- data.frame()
for (i in 1:nrow(GADM@data)){
  temp <- GADM@polygons[[i]]@labpt
  coop <- rbind(coop, temp)
}

colnames(coop) <- c("lat", "long")
#coop <- coop[c(est.area),]
coop <- cbind(coop$lat, coop$long)
coop <- coop[index,]
coop <- as.matrix(coop[, 1:2])

prdomain <- inla.nonconvex.hull(cood, -0.03, -0.05, resolution = c(100, 100))
prmesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = prdomain, max.edge = c(0.45, 1), cutoff = 0.2)
#prmesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = cood, max.edge = c(0.45, 1), cutoff = 0.2)
plot(prmesh, asp = 1, main = "")
points(cood[, 1], cood[, 2], pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "red")


A <- inla.spde.make.A(prmesh, loc = cood)
Ap <- inla.spde.make.A(prmesh, loc = coop)
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(prmesh, alpha = 2)
indexs <- inla.spde.make.index("field", spde$n.spde)

stk.e <- inla.stack(data = list(y = d$prev), A = list(A, 1), tag = "est", effects = list(c(indexs, 
                                                                                           list(Intercept = 1)), list(long = inla.group(cood[, 1]), lat = inla.group(cood[,2]))))

stk.p <- inla.stack(data = list(y = NA), A = list(Ap, 1), tag = "prd", effects = list(c(indexs, 
                                                                                           list(Intercept = 1)), list(long = inla.group(coop[, 1]), lat = inla.group(coop[,2]))))
formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + f(field, model = spde)

stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.e, stk.p)

res <- inla(formula, family = "binomial", data = inla.stack.data(stk.full), verbose = TRUE,
            control.family = list(link = "logit"),
            control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stk.full), compute = TRUE))
===========================================================

> f(id2, model = "bym2", graph =

> control.predictor = list(compute =
> TRUE))

if 'ID_2' is a copy of 'id2', then there is no need to add 'ID_2'
component, as it already is included in the bym2. the bym2 includes
both the spatial effect and the iid effect.


we'll come back shortly to #2.

>
> 3. The result of the analysis of the code is as follows, correct
> result? (I do not understand if mean is negative)

if an observation is NA, then its 'not there' and you have to tell INLA
the related family. in your case, there is only one, the binomial, and
you could use a shorthand notation

control.predictor = list(link = 1)


which 'fitted.values' will be converted to probabiltities.

the results below, uses the identity link, this is why they could be
negative.

code as follows:

You can use the SPDE approach, yes.

The SPDE model can predict, yes. At any location, including the ones you put in thorugh the data, but also at any other location.

I cannot say whether you should use the attached code for your specific needs, or not. That depends on too many unknowns for me to say yes or no to. However:

It looks from the code like you use the polygon centroid as point locations for the continuous SPDE. Is this correct? If so, note that this is an approximation you are using! If the spatial random effect is approximately constant over each polygon that should be ok. If it is not approx constant, best practice would be to use polygons instead of point locations when construcing the A matrix. I am not sure how exactly the code looks, but Finn Lindgren should know.

Last, yes. It's a possibility.

Best,
Haakon
